units.translation: b. 〈οἰόθι προτιβάλλομαι:〉 being alone I call upon you yourselves as helpers. Lᶢ
1047-52 a. 〈σχέτλιοι:〉 harsh and pitiless, and you do not change your minds when you see me falling at the knees of the queen. Lᵐ (P)
b. The meaning: when you wanted to take the fleece, you were ready to fight even all the Colchians, but now you fear the few who have come to demand me. Lᵐ
1057. 〈ἀλιτήμονος:〉 of one who has erred, that is, of an unjust one. Gᶢ
1058 a. στρευγομένοις: to those being worn out, destroyed, and distressed, or also to those lingering; whence also στράγξ, the gradual emission of water. Thus Didymus (fg I 5, 34 Schmidt 69).
b. Hence also στραγγουρία, from urinating drop by drop. P
1059. κατευκήλησεν: he stopped, brought to rest. Lᶢ (P)
1064. σταλάει: it drips; whence also σταλαγμός (a drop). Lᶢ (P)
1066. ἰκμαίνοντο: they were being moistened; from this it indicates weeping much. Lᶢ (P)
1072. προσεπτύσσετο: she was entreating, beseeching. Lᶢ P

1080-83 a. ῥέξομεν ἀμπλακίῃσιν: instead of ἁμαρτίαις (with sins). But if it is written ἀτροπίῃσιν, it means with unchangeableness. The sense: erring at first, Medea betrayed her own people and 〈...〉 she sinned by fleeing, as we often do through folly.
c. ἀκειομένη: instead of θεραπεύουσα (tending) and ἰωμένη (healing). P
1090. οἷα μὲν Ἀντιόπ〈ην〉: Antiope was the daughter of Nycteus, whom Zeus, having taken the form of a satyr, seduced, and fleeing the threats of Nycteus

she takes refuge in Sicyon with Epopeus. Having given birth to Amphion and Zethus, she exposed them on Cithaeron 〈...〉 to a certain cowherd. Nycteus, grieving because of his daughter's audacity, died, after entreating his brother Lycus not to overlook the girl, but to attack Sicyon and take her. Lycus campaigns against the city, kills Epopeus, and taking Antiope captive hands her over to Dirce, his own wife, to guard. But she flees, and being caught again is given up to her own sons. There the cowherd foster-father reveals what had happened. They save Antiope, and they destroy Dirce by tying her to a wild bull. Having summoned Lycus, as if to hand over Antiope, they were about to slaughter him; but Hermes prevented it, and ordered Lycus to yield the kingdom.
